Development · 2 min read

Build the smallest version that can teach you something

Good side projects begin with one useful question. A compact first release makes the answer visible.

Fieldnotes editorial · Sample essay

Start with a question

Before choosing a framework, write down the uncertainty your project should resolve. Can a reader find an interesting story? Can a learner return to the next lesson? A concrete question gives you a smaller, more useful first release than a long list of features.

Build one complete journey

Choose a beginning, a useful action, and a clear result. For a blog, that might mean browsing a list, opening an article, and returning to the collection. Finish that journey before adding accounts, dashboards, or comments. Each extra screen brings states that need design, implementation, and testing.

Make the result observable

Try the journey on a narrow screen and with a keyboard. Ask someone to complete it without your instructions. Notice where they hesitate, where text is unclear, and where a link leads nowhere. These observations tell you more than another week of adding features.

Let evidence choose the next step

Keep a short record of what worked and what did not. Select one improvement that removes a real obstacle, then ship again. A small release is useful when it teaches you something specific and leaves the next version easier to build.

Keep exploring

One idea leads to another.
